entities.name: The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints
entities.label: Institution
entities.summary:
The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints (LDS Church), founded in 1830 in Fayette, New York by Joseph Smith with the publication of the Book of Mormon, is the world's fastest-growing major religious denomination of the 20th century — growing from 1 million (1947) to 17 million members (2023) primarily through a worldwide 70,000-missionary program. The Church's economic infrastructure — the 10% tithing system, Deseret Industries, and Church welfare program — creates a self-sufficient member support network that has been studied by sociologists as the most effective religious community-building model in American history.

Joseph Smith claimed to have received golden plates from the angel Moroni in upstate New York, which he translated as the Book of Mormon — the record of ancient American peoples who were visited by Jesus after the Resurrection. Smith's 1844 assassination in Carthage, Illinois — where he and his brother Hyrum were killed by a mob while in jail — created the succession crisis that divided the movement and produced Brigham Young's migration of 70,000 Saints to the Salt Lake Valley (1847), establishing Utah as a Mormon-dominated territory.

The Church's 1978 revelation extending priesthood to Black members — reversing a 130-year exclusion that had become increasingly untenable — was one of the most significant ecclesiastical policy reversals in 20th-century religious history. The Church's welfare system — developed during the Great Depression — operates 400 storehouses, 97 home storage centers, and a network of canneries, farms, and employment services providing member assistance. The genealogical research program (FamilySearch) has indexed over 3 billion records — the world's largest genealogical database.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: The LDS Church's growth from 1 million to 17 million members in 76 years — driven by a worldwide 70,000-missionary program — is the fastest growth of any major religious denomination in 20th-century history, making it America's most remarkable religious export.
